c.tagline: Morocco's northern gateway — a whitewashed medina above the Strait of Gibraltar.

taxi.fareNote: Blue petits taxis handle short in-city hops (make sure the meter is on, or agree a price, before setting off) while cream grands taxis run fixed shared routes; app-based Careem has only a limited presence, so street taxis are the norm.

emergency.note: Dial 19 for police and 15 for ambulance/fire; 112 also works from mobile phones. Tourist police patrol the medina and main sights.

avoid.reason: Hustlers and fake guides at the port and medina; caution at night

hood_desc: The walled old town of narrow whitewashed lanes tumbling toward the port, packed with souks, riads, the Petit Socco cafes, and craft workshops. Best for atmosphere and first-time visitors.

The fortified hilltop quarter crowning the medina, with the Kasbah Museum (Dar el Makhzen), panoramic ramparts over the Strait, and boutique riads in restored palaces. Suits those after views and quiet charm.
The French- and Spanish-era new town around Place de France and Boulevard Pasteur, with cafes, the Terrasse des Paresseux viewpoint, banks, and modern shops. A convenient central base.
The seafront strip east of the port along the bay, lined with modern hotels, a beach promenade, and resorts stretching toward Cap Malabata. Good for beach stays and sea views.
A leafy residential plateau west of the Kasbah with early-20th-century villas, the clifftop Café Hafa overlooking the sea, and a calm local feel. Suits a quieter, authentic stay.

water.note: City tap water is chlorinated but most visitors stick to bottled.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 9-10 PM; blue petits taxis operate day and night and fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Tangier has no metro or tram. Alsa runs the modern city bus network, but most visitors rely on cheap blue petits taxis for short hops and cream grands taxis for longer shared runs. The medina and Kasbah are walk-only.
transit.pay: Pay bus fares in cash on board; petits taxis are metered (insist on the meter) and paid in cash — carry small dirham notes and coins.

bus: CTM & Supratours intercity coaches from the bus station
ferry: Fast ferries to Tarifa, Spain (Tangier Ville port, ~1 hr)
Car ferries from Tangier Med to Algeciras & Barcelona, Spain
train: ONCF Al Boraq high-speed to Rabat & Casablanca; conventional trains to Fez & Marrakech from Tangier Ville station

transit.m: Airport bus to the train station via the city centre (~40 min, fixed 40 MAD fare)
Grand taxi to city centre (fixed government tariff, ~20-25 min)

tip.r: ~5-10% at restaurants; small change (a few dirhams) for cafe waiters, porters and guides is expected.

food.name: Seafood tagine
food.desc: Strait of Gibraltar fish and shellfish cooked in a conical clay pot with chermoula, tomato, preserved lemon and olives. Tangier's defining plate.

places.name: La Saveur du Poisson
places.note: No-menu set feast ending in seafood tagine; famously rustic, arrive early or queue.

places.name: Romeo Restaurant
places.note: Affordable seafood, free bean stew to start, and well-reviewed tagines.

places.name: Chez Hassan Bab Kasbah
places.note: Cheap Kasbah-gate kitchen with tagines, grilled seafood and brochettes.

food.name: Bissara
food.desc: Thick split fava-bean soup finished with olive oil, cumin and paprika, eaten with bread for breakfast on cold mornings. Northern Morocco's comfort food.

places.name: Grand Cafe Central
places.note: Medina cafe trading since the 19th century; bissara and msemen in the morning.

places.name: Rue Siaghine breakfast counters
places.note: Small morning-only bissara stalls on the lane down from Petit Socco.

places.name: Cafe Hafa
places.note: Cliffside terraces serving bissara and mint tea over the Strait.

food.name: Pastilla
food.desc: Layered warqa pastry pie of shredded pigeon or chicken with almonds, egg and cinnamon, dusted with icing sugar. Sweet-savoury and unmistakably Moroccan.

places.name: Restaurant Hamadi
places.note: Long-running family restaurant with cushioned salons and classic Moroccan menu.

places.name: Palais Zahia
places.note: Riad dining room serving pastilla, seven-vegetable couscous and mrouzia.

places.name: Restaurant Al Maimouni
places.note: Family-run medina spot doing chicken pastilla and lamb tagine well.

food.name: Grilled sardines and fried fish
food.desc: Atlantic sardines charred over coals or a fried mixed plate of squid, prawns and small fish, eaten with cumin salt and bread. Cheap and everywhere.

places.name: Marche Central fish grills
places.note: Buy fish at the market counters and have it grilled and eaten on the spot.

places.name: Romeo Restaurant
places.note: Big plates of fried and grilled fish at low prices near the beach.

places.name: Chez Hassan Bab Kasbah
places.note: Charcoal grill turning out sardines and brochettes to a local crowd.

food.name: Msemen and harcha
food.desc: Flaky square laminated pancakes and gritty semolina griddle cakes, both eaten hot with honey, amlou or melting goat cheese for breakfast.

places.name: Grand Cafe Central
places.note: Historic cafe on the medina's main square serving msemen with mint tea.

places.name: Cafe Hafa
places.note: Open since 1921; msemen and honey on terraces above the Strait of Gibraltar.

places.name: Rue Siaghine bakeries
places.note: Morning griddle stalls making msemen and harcha to order.

food.name: Couscous
food.desc: Steamed semolina under seven vegetables and lamb, or in Tangier with fish, often finished with sweet onion and raisin tfaya. A Friday dish.

places.name: Palais Zahia
places.note: Seven-vegetable couscous with tfaya, served in a restored riad setting.

places.name: Restaurant Al Maimouni
places.note: Traditional couscous, tagines and grills cooked by the same family for years.

places.name: Restaurant Hamadi
places.note: Decades-old kitchen keeping couscous on the menu beyond Friday.

food.name: Mint tea
food.desc: Gunpowder green tea poured long over a fistful of spearmint and a great deal of sugar. Tangier cafes add a scatter of pine nuts.

places.name: Cafe Hafa
places.note: Cliff terraces open since 1921, once frequented by Bowles, Burroughs and the Stones.

places.name: Grand Cafe Central
places.note: Medina landmark on the old square; a front table is the classic Tangier seat.

places.name: Cafe Tingis
places.note: Faded old cafe facing the Central, good for watching the medina go by.

food.name: Fresh orange juice and avocado shake
food.desc: Moroccan oranges pressed by the glass, and jus d'avocat, a thick blended avocado, milk and almond shake sold at the same counters.

places.name: Grand Socco juice stands
places.note: Cluster of juice carts at the medina gate pressing oranges all day.

places.name: Cafe de Paris
places.note: 1927 cafe in the Ville Nouvelle for juice, coffee and old Tangier atmosphere.

places.name: Marche Central juice counters
places.note: Market bars blending avocado, banana and almond shakes to order.

landmarks: Kasbah and Kasbah Museum (Dar el Makhzen)
The fortified hilltop quarter's former sultan's palace, now a museum of Moroccan artistry, guarding sweeping views over the Strait of Gibraltar.
Tangier Medina
A whitewashed maze tumbling toward the port, where writers from Bowles to Burroughs found inspiration among souks, cafés and blue-shuttered lanes.
Caves of Hercules
A legendary sea grotto at Cape Spartel whose opening famously mirrors the map of Africa, linked to myths of the resting demigod.
Cap Spartel
The dramatic lighthouse-topped promontory where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean, marking Africa's northwestern tip amid pine forests.
Café Hafa
A 1921 cliffside terrace of cascading blue-and-white tiers, where the Rolling Stones and generations of artists have sipped mint tea over sea views.
American Legation Museum
The first American public property abroad, a labyrinthine medina mansion of art and history commemorating US-Moroccan friendship since 1821.
Grand Socco (Place du 9 Avril 1947)
The palm-ringed plaza bridging old and new Tangier, buzzing around its fountain beneath the tiled minaret of Sidi Bou Abib Mosque.
Petit Socco
The medina's storied little square, once notorious in Tangier's freewheeling International Zone days, now perfect for people-watching over coffee.
St Andrew's Church
A charming 1905 Anglican church built in Moorish style, its Lord's Prayer carved in Arabic and its garden cemetery full of Tangier characters.
Perdicaris Park (Rmilat Forest)
A romantic clifftop woodland estate west of town, its eucalyptus trails and ruined mansion overlooking the Strait's shimmering shipping lanes.

train.note: ONCF's Al Boraq high-speed line reaches Rabat (~1h30) and Casablanca (~2h10) from Tangier Ville; conventional trains continue to Fez, Meknès and Marrakech.

intl.to: European cities via ferry (CTM international coaches)

bus.note: CTM and Supratours run intercity coaches from Tangier to Chefchaouen (~2h), Tetouan, Fez, Rabat and Casablanca; the modern Gare Routière bus station sits south of the centre.

intl.to: Tarifa, Spain (fast ferry, ~1 hr, from Tangier Ville port)
Algeciras & Barcelona, Spain (car ferries from Tangier Med, ~45 km east)

ferry.note: Tangier is the main sea gateway between Africa and Europe: fast ferries cross the Strait of Gibraltar to Tarifa from the central Tangier Ville port, while larger car ferries to Algeciras and Barcelona leave from Tangier Med.

half.name: Asilah
half.blurb: A whitewashed, blue-trimmed coastal town 45 km south, known for its ramparts, mural-covered medina and beaches.

full.name: Chefchaouen
full.blurb: Morocco's famous blue-painted mountain town in the Rif, about 2 hours south — a maze of indigo lanes and craft shops.

full.name: Tetouan
full.blurb: A UNESCO-listed Andalusian medina about an hour east, with strong Spanish-Moorish heritage and a lively souk.

full.name: Tarifa, Spain
full.blurb: A quick fast-ferry hop across the Strait to Europe's southern tip — a windsurfing town with old-town charm and Roman ruins nearby.
